title: Business Processes: Stakeholders, Change, Teams, and Service Catalog
bodyMarkdown:
## Why this matters for the PCA exam

A large share of the business-process sub-objective is about people. The exam describes anxious operators, a mandated deadline, a team new to Kubernetes, a platform handed over with no follow-up, or application teams provisioning inconsistent infrastructure, and asks what a good architect does first. The answers reward engagement, enablement, phased and reversible change, evidence-based decisions and lightweight governance. They penalize mandates, silent cutovers, ignoring skills and measuring only uptime. The Well-Architected [operational excellence pillar](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/operational-excellence) frames the technical counterpart in five principles: ensure operational readiness and performance using CloudOps, manage incidents and problems, manage and optimize cloud resources, automate and manage change, and continuously improve and innovate. It also stresses a cultural shift toward continuous learning, experimentation and team empowerment.

## Stakeholder management

Identify stakeholders early and map what each cares about:

| Stakeholder | Typical concern | How to engage |
|---|---|---|
| Executive sponsor | Business value, risk, timeline | Outcome and risk framing, milestones, quarterly reviews |
| Security and compliance | Controls, audit evidence, data residency | Involve at design time; show guardrails and audit logs |
| Finance | Forecast, unit cost, CapEx to OpEx change | Budgets, labels, showback or chargeback reports |
| Operations and SRE | Toil, on-call load, runbooks, reliability | Early hands-on access, training, clear ownership |
| Application owners | Delivery speed, migration effort | Self-service paths, migration help, realistic schedules |
| End users | Continuity, performance | Communication of changes, phased rollout |

Practical principles:

- **Facilitate rather than dictate.** Put trade-offs among cost, performance, risk and timeline in front of the people who own the decision, with options and a recommendation.
- **Speak each audience's language.** Executives hear ROI and risk; operators hear toil reduction and on-call impact.
- **Keep a cadence.** Regular touchpoints avoid the failure mode of disappearing until launch.
- **Escalate last.** Engage and unblock first; escalate when engagement has failed, not as the opening move.

## Change management

Technology programs usually fail for human reasons. A reliable sequence:

1. **Communicate the why.** Explain the business benefit and what changes for each group.
2. **Train and enable.** Close skills gaps before cutover, not after.
3. **Phase the rollout.** Pilots, canaries and reversible steps limit risk. Cloud Run, for instance, supports gradual rollout, such as 1% of requests to a new revision while monitoring telemetry, per the [Cloud Run overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run).
4. **Gather feedback and respond visibly.** People accept change they have influenced.
5. **Approve and record.** Production changes go through a recorded approval; for deployments that can be a Cloud Deploy target with `requireApproval` where any user or service account holding `roles/clouddeploy.approver` can approve, per the [Cloud Deploy approvals documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deploy/docs/promote-release).
6. **Review outcomes.** Confirm the expected benefit materialized and adjust.

### Governance without gridlock

Approvals should be proportionate. DORA's research on [streamlining change approval](https://dora.dev/capabilities/streamlining-change-approval/) found that heavyweight external approval had a negative effect on software delivery performance and no evidence of lower change fail rates. Its recommendation is peer review captured in the development platform, plus automated testing, continuous integration and monitoring to catch bad changes early. A change advisory board is better used for notification, coordination and process improvement than for reviewing code. Reserve human gates for high-risk or regulated changes and automate the rest.

For the audit trail, [Cloud Audit Logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit) records who did what: Admin Activity logs are always written and cannot be disabled, and Data Access logs are off by default except for BigQuery. That gives auditors evidence without adding manual steps.

### Learning culture

Google SRE's [postmortem culture](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) chapter ties change to psychological safety: blameless postmortems let people escalate without fear, and recognition programs, leadership participation, reading clubs and "Wheel of Misfortune" exercises reinforce the behavior. Resistance to a migration is often fear of losing competence, so the first response is enablement and listening, not a mandate.

## Team assessment and skills readiness

Compare the skills the target architecture requires with what the team has. The decision has two branches, and they are not exclusive:

| Option | When it fits | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Close the gap | The technology is strategically right and there is time | Training, certification, pairing with experts, a pilot service, an internal guild |
| Reduce the operational burden | The gap is large or time is short | Choose more managed services |

On the managed side, [GKE Autopilot](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/autopilot-overview) has Google manage nodes, scaling, security patching and upgrades, with a default hardened configuration and an SLA covering both control plane and Pod compute capacity; general-purpose workloads are billed per Pod resource requests. Choose Standard instead when you need manual control or flexibility that Autopilot constraints prevent. [Cloud Run](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/overview/what-is-cloud-run) goes further: no cluster to create or manage, and instances scale to zero when there are no requests. For a team with limited container experience, "assess the gap, then train or favor a more managed option" is the pattern; "choose the hardest option to force learning" is a trap.

## Decision-making processes

- **Define criteria first,** then score options: cost, risk, time, security, team capability, reversibility.
- **Document the decision.** Google's guidance on [architecture decision records](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/architecture-decision-records) describes an ADR as capturing the key options, the main requirements that drive the decision and the decision itself. Typical sections include context, functional and non-functional requirements, impacted critical user journeys, key options and the decision rationale with a timestamp. Store ADRs near the application code, ideally in the same version control system, often as Markdown. ADRs help onboarding and avoid repeating the same discussions.
- **Prefer reversible steps under uncertainty.** A pilot or canary migration beats a big-bang decision.
- **Revisit decisions when assumptions change,** and mark old ADRs superseded rather than deleting them.

## Customer success management

Customer success, for an architect, means the business realizes the value that justified the project:

- **Agree success metrics at the start:** adoption, time to provision, cost per unit of work, reliability targets, business KPIs.
- **Track realized value,** not only uptime. A perfectly available platform nobody uses has failed.
- **Hold regular reviews** (for example quarterly) to review adoption, incidents, cost and roadmap, and to feed lessons back.
- **Treat go-live as the start of value realization.** The engagement is not finished when the platform is deployed.

Google's support tiers are the vendor-side counterpart. Per the Customer Care docs, [Standard Support](https://docs.cloud.google.com/support/docs/standard) is business-hours, English-only, with a four-hour first response on P2 cases. [Enhanced Support](https://docs.cloud.google.com/support/docs/enhanced) adds 24/7 coverage for higher priorities and a one-hour first response on P1; a Technical Account Advisor service is an optional add-on. [Premium Support](https://docs.cloud.google.com/support/docs/premium) gives P1 cases a 15-minute first response 24/7 and a dedicated Technical Account Manager (TAM) who helps with onboarding, cloud maturity assessment, operational health reviews and cost guidance. Premium also includes event management for planned peak events (system preparation, load testing, disaster recovery testing, post-event review) with a 30-day lead time, and Customer Aware Support, where Google holds architecture details of your environment. Recommend Premium for mission-critical production with launch events and a need for proactive guidance; Standard suits dev and non-critical workloads. Support is reactive by itself, so the TAM relationship, your success metrics and the quarterly review together are what make the engagement proactive.

## Service catalog and provisioning

The goal is autonomy with standards: teams self-serve approved, compliant building blocks instead of filing tickets or, worse, being handed broad roles such as Project Owner. Google Cloud offers several pieces, and the exam tests which one fits.

| Need | Service | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| Curated, approved solutions that developers discover and launch | [Service Catalog](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-catalog/docs/overview) | Admins publish catalogs at organization, folder or project level; respects organization policies |
| Declarative Terraform deployments as a managed service | [Infrastructure Manager](https://docs.cloud.google.com/infrastructure-manager/docs/overview) | Runs Terraform in an ephemeral Cloud Build environment; revisions, previews and stored state |
| Reusable, governed application templates | [Application Design Center](https://docs.cloud.google.com/application-design-center/docs/overview) | Platform teams publish templates in catalogs and spaces; developers customize drafts |
| Finding services at runtime across environments | [Service Directory](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-directory/docs/overview) | Registry of namespaces, services and endpoints, resolvable over DNS, HTTP or gRPC |

**Service Catalog.** The [solution types](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-catalog/docs/manage-solutions) are Terraform configurations, Deployment Manager based solutions and link-based solutions. Users [launch](https://docs.cloud.google.com/service-catalog/docs/view-and-launch) them with the Catalog Consumer or Viewer role, and Terraform solutions run through Cloud Build, using either the default Cloud Build service account or one the user specifies, so that account needs permission on the target resources. That is the control point: users get the ability to deploy the approved template without holding broad roles themselves. Updating the configuration in Cloud Storage surfaces a new version to users.

**Infrastructure Manager.** It stores Terraform state and logs in a Cloud Storage bucket it creates, versions each change as a revision (`r-0`, `r-1`, and so on), and offers [previews](https://docs.cloud.google.com/infrastructure-manager/docs/preview-deployment) that execute `terraform plan` without changing resources, including drift detail. Use it when you want Terraform run centrally with a service account, an audit trail and no self-managed pipeline. It is also the migration target for Deployment Manager: [Google discontinued Deployment Manager support on April 1, 2026](https://docs.cloud.google.com/deployment-manager/docs/deprecations) and recommends Infrastructure Manager, with the DM Convert tool to translate configurations. Any answer that starts a new estate on Deployment Manager is wrong.

**Choosing.** Service Catalog is the answer for "let developers self-serve approved solutions"; Infrastructure Manager for "run our Terraform as a managed, reviewed deployment"; Application Design Center for "platform team publishes governed application blueprints"; Service Directory for "services across Google Cloud, on-premises and other clouds need one registry and consistent names," not for provisioning. Anti-patterns: a wiki of copy-paste snippets, Terraform state on laptops, and unreviewed applies from a developer's machine.

## Measuring whether the change worked

Change management needs evidence, not impressions. Pair adoption and satisfaction signals with delivery metrics: the [DORA metrics](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/) of change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate show whether a new process makes delivery faster and safer or merely different. Review them before and after the change, and share the results with the same stakeholders you engaged at the start. If lead time improved but change fail rate rose, the story for executives and operators is not "success" but "we need more automated verification," and that is a legitimate outcome of the feedback loop.

A worked pattern for a mixed scenario: a retailer moves a legacy order system to Google Cloud. The architect meets security, finance, operations and application owners in week one and records the decision criteria in an ADR. Operations staff pair with the platform team on a low-risk pilot service running on Cloud Run, which removes cluster management from the first learning curve. Application teams receive Service Catalog templates for approved databases and networks. Production releases require a Cloud Deploy approval while lower environments promote automatically. After go-live, a quarterly review tracks adoption, cost per order, incidents and DORA metrics, and the roadmap changes accordingly.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Mandate and escalate.** Imposing a deadline and escalating resistance destroys trust and slows adoption.
- **Silent weekend cutover.** No communication, no training, no rollback story.
- **Outsourcing or replacing the team** to avoid the training conversation.
- **Ignoring team skills** because the technology choice is "purely technical."
- **Gatekeeper-heavy approvals** for every change, which slows delivery and does not lower failure rates.
- **Declaring victory at go-live** and measuring only infrastructure uptime.
- **Undocumented decisions,** which get relitigated at every staff change.
- **Over-privileged self-service,** such as Project Owner for everyone, instead of curated templates.
- **Buying the top support tier for everything,** or skipping it for a mission-critical launch; match the tier to the criticality of the workload.
- **Stakeholder blindness:** talking only to the sponsor and meeting security, finance and operations for the first time at launch.

## Exam tips

- **Resistant operations team:** engage early with a change-management plan: communicate the why, train, gather feedback. Never mandate, escalate first, or cut over silently.
- **Limited container skills:** assess the gap, then train or favor managed options such as Cloud Run or GKE Autopilot.
- **Customer success** means success metrics agreed with stakeholders, tracked adoption and value KPIs, and regular reviews, not uptime alone and not ending at deployment.
- **Pre-approved self-service templates:** Service Catalog, not shared wiki snippets, Marketplace public listings or Project Owner for all. Managed Terraform with previews and state is Infrastructure Manager, which replaces Deployment Manager (support discontinued April 1, 2026); Service Directory is runtime discovery, not provisioning.
- **Support tiers:** Standard is business hours; Enhanced adds 24/7 with a one-hour P1 response; Premium adds a 15-minute P1 response, a dedicated TAM and event management. A TAM suits proactive customer success for critical workloads.
- **Phase, pilot, canary, reversible:** the preferred rollout shape for both software and organizational change.
- **Approvals proportionate to risk:** a recorded gate for production; DORA says heavyweight external boards do not reduce change failures.
- **Document with ADRs** stored with the code: options, requirements, decision, rationale.
- **Audit trail** comes from Cloud Audit Logs and recorded approvals, not manual spreadsheets.

diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  Why["Communicate the why"] --> Train["Train and enable"]
  Train --> Pilot["Phased pilot or canary"]
  Pilot --> Feedback["Gather feedback and adjust"]
  Feedback --> Approve{"Approval gate for production"}
  Approve --> Rollout["Production rollout"]
  Rollout --> Review["Customer success review"]
  Review -->|"Lessons"| Why

diagrams.title: Aligning technology with team readiness
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Assess team skills against target architecture"] --> Q{"Skills gap?"}
  Q -->|"No"| Go["Proceed with the chosen platform"]
  Q -->|"Yes"| Opt{"Time and appetite to close it?"}
  Opt -->|"Yes"| Train["Train, certify and run a pilot"]
  Opt -->|"No"| Managed["Prefer managed options: Cloud Run or GKE Autopilot"]
  Train --> ADR["Record the decision in an ADR"]
  Managed --> ADR
  Go --> ADR
